items.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
items.summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

ByGeeta Pandey

Women & Social Affairs Editor, India

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.

More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed

South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

• In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage

• Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict

• India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.

Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries

"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."

The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

• India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it

• India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.

"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."

Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

items.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
items.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence company Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo

ByDavide Ghiglione, in Rome and Laura Gozzi

Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.

His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.

In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.

The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.

But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.

In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.

The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Gianni De Gennaro (L) and anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in 1992

"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.

The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.

The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.

On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.

"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.

The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.

The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".

Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

Iran warned South Korea that an expanded foreign military presence in the Gulf could heighten tensions and widen the conflict.

SEOUL: Iran's foreign minister has told his South Korean counterpart that a foreign military presence in the Gulf region would heighten tensions rather than contribute to peace, as Seoul prepares to expand the operational area of a navy unit to waters south of the Gulf of Oman.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke by telephone on Thursday (Nov 26) with South Korea's Cho Hyun, who reaffirmed Seoul did not intend to join any war or deploy troops to the Gulf, the Iranian embassy in Seoul said in an X post on Friday.

South Korea's parliament is reviewing a government motion to broaden the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to include the outer waters of the Gulf of Oman to help ensure safe navigation of its commercial vessels.

The anti-piracy Cheonghae unit has been stationed in the Gulf of Aden since 2009.

Araqchi said the presence of foreign militaries "would instead heighten tensions and expand the scope of conflict", the Iranian embassy said.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry said Cho explained that the mission of the navy unit was to ensure the safety of South Koreans and protect the country's economic interests.

South Korea, which is one of the world's largest oil and gas importers, sourced 70 per cent of its oil from the Middle East in 2025, with most shipments delivered through the Strait of Hormuz, according to government data.

items.title: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
items.summary: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
items.body:
Obituaries

Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died

November 27, 20261:12 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin, July 16, 2008.

Franka Bruns/AP

hide caption

Franka Bruns/AP

Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.

His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.

FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993.

James Finley/AP

hide caption

James Finley/AP

Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."

Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.

Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

斯特罗布·塔尔博特，曾任《时代》杂志记者，后于比尔·克林顿总统任内担任副国务卿，之后又执掌布鲁金斯学会，于周四去世，享年80岁。

其子德文·塔尔博特证实，他在纽约州东汉普顿的家中久病之后安详离世。

老塔尔博特曾就读于耶鲁大学和牛津大学，在牛津期间与克林顿同住。在英国求学时，他曾在《时代》杂志莫斯科分社实习，随后该杂志请她协助翻译尼基塔·赫鲁晓夫泄露的回忆录。赫鲁晓夫是苏联共产党前第一书记，于1964年被赶下台。

资料图——1993年1月2日，当选总统比尔·克林顿与《时代》杂志的斯特罗布·塔尔博特在南卡罗来纳州希尔顿黑德岛的海滩上散步时私下交谈。

James Finley/美联社

隐藏图注

James Finley/美联社

塔尔博特完成了这项工作，这让他年纪轻轻便小有名气，并因此获得了该杂志的一份工作。

据美国国务院为其撰写的传记，他在《时代》杂志工作了21年，主要关注苏美关系，曾任华盛顿分社社长和外交事务专栏作家。此后，他接到了刚刚当选的克林顿的电话。

塔尔博特于1994年加入美国国务院，很快升任副国务卿。在这一职位上，他是克林顿政府对俄及其他前苏联国家政策的制定者，并在1998年印度核试验后主持了美印之间的谈判。

“斯特罗布是一位善良而杰出的人，他让我们的世界更加和平与安全，”克林顿在塔尔博特去世后发表的一份声明中说。他说，塔尔博特在牛津翻译赫鲁晓夫回忆录时，每天为他做早餐是克林顿的任务，并补充道：“不知怎的，我占了便宜。”

他说，他和希拉里都对“一位了不起的朋友、一位世界级人物的离去”“深感悲痛”。

此后，他于2002年至2017年担任布鲁金斯学会主席。在此期间，他还主持了美国国务院外交事务政策委员会。

塔尔博特还著有十余本书。他的最后一本书名为《我们国父的警告：理性时代遇上特朗普时代》，于2020年出版。

他1946年出生于俄亥俄州代顿，身后留下两个儿子德文和阿德里安，以及六个孙辈。

他的第一任妻子布鲁克·希勒于2009年去世，他后来与作家芭芭拉·拉齐尔·阿舍结婚。

items.title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
items.summary: Aid for Ukraine was among the disputes as EU members hope to conclude talks by the end of the year.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to reduce EU spending

ByHarry Sekulich

European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.

Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.

Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.

Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.

"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.

"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.

EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.

Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.

Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.

Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.

Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.

Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.

European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.

French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".

Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."

Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.

Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

Could housing decide Spain's general election?

Housing has been the biggest issue for voters ahead of Spain's general election on Sunday, with millions of people protesting across the country in recent weeks over a lack of affordable homes.

items.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
items.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number

ByNawal Al-Maghafi

Senior international investigations correspondent, Reporting fromRiyadh

Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters

Image caption,

Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.

He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.

He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.

"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."

The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.

According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.

Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.

In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.

As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.

Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

Image source, Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

Image caption,

Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.

As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.

The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.

Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.

The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

Image source, BBC/Liam Weir

Image caption,

Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal

Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.

But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.

Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.

We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

Image source, BBC/Liam Weir

Image caption,

Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.

"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."

Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November

The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.

Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.

The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.

Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.
One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

blocks.alt: Grainy footage with a pinkish hue shows people trying to leave the airport building where there is smoke, fire and damaged fittings.

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters
Image caption,
Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.
He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.
He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.
"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."
The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.
According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.
Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.
In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.
Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

blocks.alt: Map showing the location of Saudi Arabia with Yemen to the south, the Red Sea to the west and Iran across the Gulf to the east. Sanaa, Taiz and Aden are marked in south-west Yemen. Riyadh is roughly in the middle of Saudi Arabia with Dammam to its east and Medina to its west.

blocks.text: For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.
As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.
Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

blocks.alt: An external shot of a section of a skyscraper with damaged walls and windows. Part of about six floors appears to be damaged. The sky behind it is bright blue.

blocks.text: Image source, Saudi Press Agency/Reuters
Image caption,
Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.
As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.
The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.
Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.
Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.
The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

blocks.alt: A stallholder in a market is showing man some watches. The seller has short dark hair, a short beard and a moustache. Behind him are other stalls and shops.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Liam Weir
Image caption,
Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal
Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.
But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.
Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.
We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

blocks.alt: A man with shortish greying hair looks at the camera. He is wearing a black polo-neck top. He is outside with palm trees, neat grass and hedges behind him and a white building with arches to the left.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Liam Weir
Image caption,
Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.
"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."
Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

blocks.alt: A destroyed warehouse with most of the roof caved in. Some of the walls have also collapsed. There are beams and bits of debris hanging from the remains of the roof. Six people are standing in front of the building surrounded by debris.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Image caption,
The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November
The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.
Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.
The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.
Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

items.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
items.summary: The struggle many face in buying a home has been the biggest issue of a bitter campaign.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing struggles

ByNick Beake

Europe correspondent, Reporting fromValencia

Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.

Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.

The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.

The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.

If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.

Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.

Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.

Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

• Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stakePublished1 day ago

Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.

But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.

"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.

She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.

Image caption,

Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out

"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.

We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.

This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.

One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.

Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.

Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.

"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.

"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."

The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.

Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.

Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.

Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.

Image source, Europa Press via Getty Images

Image caption,

Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate

On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.

On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".

Image caption,

Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time

Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.

But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.

"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.

"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."

Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.

"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.

We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.

Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?

"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."

Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.

In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.

Vox called it an "invasion".

Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.

Image caption,

Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party

In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.

Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.

"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.

"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"

Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.

I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.

María shakes her head.

"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.

"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."

Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.

He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.

The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

items.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
items.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning her relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives

BySimon Atkinson

Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.

Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".

She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.

Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.

She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.

She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.

Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

澳大利亚蘑菇杀手艾琳·帕特森已发起最后的法律努力，试图推翻其谋杀罪名并避免死于狱中。

52岁的艾琳·帕特森去年被判罪名成立，罪名是2023年她在一顿掺有毒蘑菇的餐食中谋杀三名亲属并企图杀害另一人。

上个月，在维多利亚州上诉法院，三名法官驳回了对她定罪的上诉，并排除了她获得假释的可能性——称她的罪行“极其冷酷且蓄意”，必须“以最强烈的措辞予以谴责”。

她现已向高等法院提出最后申请，要求审理她的案件。

帕特森有28天时间提交向高等法院申请上诉特别许可，该截止日期已于周五到期。

她希望该国最高法官同时审查她的定罪和量刑——但法院不必同意审理此案。法院只审理约10%的上诉案件。

在去年一场备受关注的审判后，陪审团裁定帕特森罪名成立，认定她通过向公婆唐和盖尔·帕特森以及盖尔的妹妹希瑟·威尔金森分别提供含有毒鹅膏菌的惠灵顿牛排而谋杀他们，这些蘑菇是她追踪、采集并烹制的。

帕特森还被判企图谋杀希瑟的丈夫伊恩·威尔金森罪名成立，伊恩是当地牧师，他也在帕特森位于维多利亚州乡村的家中食用了那顿有毒午餐。

他在住院数周后幸存，但因中毒仍有持续的健康问题。

女主人的分居丈夫西蒙·帕特森本应参加那顿午餐，但在最后一刻取消，部分原因是他相信妻子多年来多次试图毒害他。

帕特森于去年9月被判刑，主审法官考虑到她可能面临的“严酷监狱条件”，允许33年的非假释期。这一线自由的希望被上诉法官驳回，他们裁定她永远不应获释。

她曾以七项理由主张其定罪不安全——包括一次酒店预订混乱，导致陪审团与控方、一名关键警方证人和媒体住在同一地点。

她的律师称这是“灾难性的”，损害了审判的公正性，但上诉法院法官驳回了所有上诉理由。
